name: Luferlang
description: The Luferlang is a 'fearsome critter' of North American logging-camp tall tales, recorded in Henry H. Tryon's 1939 Fearsome Critters as a hideous equine beast with triple-jointed legs that allow it to run equally fast in any direction, a dark blue dorsal stripe, a swivel-jointed tail set in the middle of its back, and a single deadly bite delivered only once a year.
full_description: The Luferlang (also Lufferlang) is a creature of North American logging-camp folklore, belonging to the genre known as 'fearsome critters'. Its canonical description is from Henry H. Tryon's 1939 Fearsome Critters: a horse-like beast with all four legs triple-jointed, allowing it to run equally fast in any direction, a dark blue stripe down the spine, and a bushy, swivel-jointed tail set in the middle of its back. It is reputed to be exceptionally dangerous and likely to attack without provocation, but bites only once a year — though, the tradition holds, that single bite is invariably fatal. The standard defences cited by Tryon are unusually specific: holding up a large mirror so the doubled image confuses the beast and drives it off, or wearing or displaying an orange-coloured handkerchief, which is said to give 'full protection'. Like other fearsome critters — the Hodag, the Snoligoster, the Hidebehind, the Squonk — the Luferlang originated as an oral tall-tale tradition in the logging camps of the Great Lakes and northeast United States, used to entertain seasoned loggers and to haze new recruits. It survives almost entirely as a literary tradition, principally through Tryon's book.
origin: A creature of the oral tradition of North American logging camps, with no fixed real-world range. Tryon (1939) places fearsome critters generally in the forests of the northern United States and Canada.

etymology.origin: Coined within North American logging-camp oral tradition; the etymology is opaque and not given in the cited literature. The word's first published appearance in cryptid bestiaries is in Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters (1939).
etymology.meaning: Not glossed in the original sources.

timeline.event: William T. Cox publishes Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, codifying the genre but not including the Luferlang
Henry H. Tryon publishes Fearsome Critters, including the canonical Luferlang entry
timeline.significance: Earliest known print appearance of the Luferlang
timeline.source: Wikipedia, Fearsome critters; Tryon, H. H. (1939)

cultural_notes: Audiences of these tall tales never literally believed in fearsome critters; the tradition functions as occupational humour and initiation.
